Title: Passage 1: A Day in the Life of a Park Ranger in Glacier National Park
Author: by the National Park Service
Content: Glacier National Park is a busy place in the `text(summer)`. There are about `text(2 million)` visitors that come to enjoy the beauty of Glacier. To help us protect this special place, Glacier has several types of park rangers. Some rangers protect Glacier National Park by enforcing its laws and regulations. . . . Some rangers protect the park by educating visitors about all the wonderful things about Glacier National Park. Some rangers patrol the trails to make sure that visitors are safe and trails are in good condition.

A ranger’s job is to protect all that is within Glacier National Park from harm. This can be very exciting because you never know what you might do in a `text(day)`. A ranger might help a visitor who needs some directions to the Visitor Center. . . .
A ranger can be called on a Search and Rescue `text(day)` or night, so they must always have their rescue gear ready to go. Rescues can take a couple `text(hours)` to several `text(weeks)`. . . .

The job of some rangers is to teach the visitors all about Glacier National Park. They may work in a Visitor Center, lead hikes, give programs to kids, and perform campfire talks and slide programs in the evening. Their job is to help visitors understand and care about Glacier National Park.

Backcountry rangers hike the trails every `text(day)`. They check the trails to make sure that there are no hazards, such as a tree that is across the trail. If a tree is across the trail, the ranger will use a saw to cut it out. The rangers also talk to visitors that are backcountry camping and make sure they are safe and following the rules. Backcountry rangers will often use horses when they travel the trail. Sometimes rangers will spend up to `text(10 days)` camping before coming out of the backcountry.
